title: 09. Storage, CDN & Data Engineering: Distributed File Systems

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A distributed file system (DFS) spreads a single logical filesystem across many commodity servers, striping large files into fixed-size chunks that are replicated across multiple nodes so that the cluster survives disk, rack, and node failures while scaling to petabytes of capacity and gigabytes-per-second of throughput.

A distributed file system is what you build when a single NFS filer can no longer hold your data. The motivating problem is simple: by the mid-2000s Yahoo, Google, and Facebook each had more than a petabyte of web-crawl, click, and log data, and no single disk array could store it, no single server could read it fast enough, and no commercial SAN could be purchased at a price any of them would pay. The answer was to take thousands of cheap commodity boxes — each with four to twelve SATA disks and a gigabit NIC — and stitch them into a single filesystem that an application could address as one big tree. The two foundational designs are Google's GFS (2003 paper) and Apache HDFS (2006, a clean-room reimplementation of GFS), and almost every modern distributed filesystem — CephFS, GlusterFS, MooseFS, Quantcast FS — borrows the same shape: a small metadata service that tracks the directory tree and chunk locations, and a large pool of data nodes that store the actual bytes.

The architecture is intentionally split between metadata and data. A file in HDFS is not a contiguous run of blocks on one disk; it is a sequence of 128MB chunks (called "blocks" in HDFS, "chunks" in GFS), each chunk independently placed on a different data node, and each chunk replicated to three nodes by default. The NameNode holds the namespace tree (directories, file names, permissions) and a mapping from each file to the list of chunk IDs and the data nodes that hold replicas. When a client wants to read `/logs/2024/03/pageviews.parquet`, it asks the NameNode for the chunk list, picks the closest replica for each chunk (rack-aware placement prefers the same rack to save cross-rack bandwidth), and streams the bytes directly from DataNodes — the NameNode is never on the hot path. Writes go the other way: the client picks a DataNode for the first replica, that DataNode pipelines the chunk to the second, which pipelines to the third, and an acknowledgment flows back. This pipeline gives replication for durability without a separate copy step, and it explains why HDFS write throughput is bounded by the slowest replica in the pipeline.

The defining trade-off of a DFS is throughput-over-latency. HDFS is built for batch: a MapReduce job reading terabytes of log data wants sequential read throughput of 100+ MB/s per node, and it does not care that the first byte of the first read takes 30ms (NameNode RPC, plus DataNode seek). The same design that delivers 100 GB/s of aggregate cluster throughput is unusable for an OLTP database doing 4KB random reads at 10,000 IOPS — there is no random read cache, no foreground write coalescing, no sub-millisecond latency target. GFS's original paper notes that the system targeted "large streaming reads and writes" and explicitly "did not optimize for small reads or writes," and HDFS inherits this. The chunk size itself (128MB) is a giveaway: a 128MB chunk amortizes NameNode metadata cost (one chunk ID per 128MB, not per 4KB block), but it means the smallest file in HDFS still occupies 128MB of metadata-planning space, which is why HDFS administrators tell you "don't store a billion small files."

The real-world example that crystallizes the pattern is Yahoo's HDFS cluster, which by 2009 ran more than 4,000 nodes holding 25 PB of web index and click data, running Hadoop MapReduce jobs to produce Yahoo's search index. Every night the crawl pipeline wrote tens of terabytes of new HTML and click logs into HDFS, MapReduce jobs transformed them into inverted indexes, and the indexes were pushed out to the search frontends. The cluster tolerated two to three node failures per day on average — disks died, NICs flaked, kernels panicked — and the NameNode simply re-replicated the chunks from the surviving replicas to new nodes, keeping the replication factor at three. The economics were the point: at 2009 prices, 25 PB on a commercial SAN would have cost tens of millions of dollars; 4,000 commodity boxes cost about a tenth of that, and Yahoo could add capacity in $5,000 increments as needed. This is the canonical DFS win — petabyte scale, commodity hardware, software tolerance for failure.

The Netflix migration from HDFS to S3 is the canonical counter-example. Netflix ran HDFS clusters for years to back their recommendation and analytics pipelines, but by 2015 they were running clusters at the 1 PB+ scale across three AWS regions, and operating HDFS on top of EC2 was painful: rebalancing a cluster after node churn took days, NameNode memory became a bottleneck as the file count grew, and the operational burden of managing 1,000-node HDFS clusters did not differentiate Netflix's business. They migrated to S3 + EMRFS (Hadoop's S3 filesystem implementation), trading the NameNode bottleneck and rebalancing pain for S3's essentially-infinite capacity and zero-ops durability. The trade-off they accepted: S3 has no `append`, no rename atomicity across "directories," and 20–50ms latency per operation — workloads that needed HDFS's append semantics (like writing log files in real time) had to be rewritten to buffer and write complete files. The lesson is that DFS is the right layer when you need POSIX-ish semantics (append, random read, hierarchical directories) at petabyte scale on hardware you control; object storage is the right layer when you want petabyte scale without operating a cluster.

CephFS and GlusterFS represent a third branch: distributed filesystems that target general-purpose POSIX workloads, not just batch analytics. CephFS sits on top of Ceph's RADOS object store, with a metadata cluster (MDS) that can scale horizontally by sharding directories across multiple MDS instances, and a CRUSH algorithm that computes chunk placement deterministically (no central lookup needed). GlusterFS uses a "translator stack" approach where each brick (a directory on a node) is combined with translators for replication, distribution, and caching. These systems try to deliver both the scale-out of HDFS and the POSIX semantics of NFS, but they are harder to operate than either — CephFS in particular had reputation for instability through the late 2010s, and is most often used for OpenStack and HPC workloads where the deployment team is sophisticated. The architectural takeaway: pick the DFS that matches your workload — HDFS for batch analytics on a Hadoop/Spark stack, CephFS for general-purpose POSIX at scale on OpenStack, GlusterFS for media streaming with simple replication, and S3-backed (JuiceFS, Mountpoint, EMRFS) for cloud-native workloads that want zero-ops storage.

sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD C[Client App
MapReduce/Spark] -->|get chunk locations| NN[NameNode
metadata: tree + chunk map] NN -->|chunk IDs + replica nodes| C C -->|read chunk 1| DN1[DataNode 1
rack 1] C -->|read chunk 2| DN2[DataNode 2
rack 2] C -->|read chunk 3| DN3[DataNode 3
rack 1] DN1 -.->|pipeline replicate| DN2 DN2 -.->|pipeline replicate| DN3[DataNode 3
rack 2] NN <-->|block reports
heartbeats every 3s| DN1 NN <-->|block reports
heartbeats| DN2 NN <-->|block reports
heartbeats| DN3 F[Failed DataNode] -.->|missed heartbeat 10s| NN NN -.->|re-replicate under-replicated chunks| DN4[New DataNode] ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------+ +---------------------------------+ | Client |------->| NameNode (metadata) | | (MR/Spark) | RPC | tree: /logs/2024/pageviews.par | +------+------+ | file=42 -> [c1, c2, c3, c4] | | | c1 -> [DN1, DN2, DN5] (rf=3) | | | c2 -> [DN2, DN3, DN1] | | chunk locations +-----+-------+ | | v v +-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+ | DataNode 1 | | DataNode 2 | | DataNode 3 | | chunk c1 * |=====>| chunk c1 * |=====>| chunk c2 * | | chunk c2 * | | chunk c2 * | | (rack 2) | | (rack 1) | | (rack 2) | +-------------+ +-------------+ +-------------+ Legend: * = primary replica, ===> = pipeline replication Failure: DN1 dies -> NameNode sees missed heartbeat (10s) -> marks c1,c2 under-replicated -> tells DN4,DN5 to copy from surviving replicas -> rf=3 restored within minutes ``` ### Walkthrough 1. A client opens a large file (e.g., `/logs/2024/pageviews.parquet`) by asking the NameNode for the list of chunk IDs and their replica locations; the NameNode returns the metadata in one RPC and steps out of the data path. 2. For each chunk, the client connects to the closest replica (rack-aware placement prefers same-rack nodes), reads sequentially at 100+ MB/s, and streams the bytes into the MapReduce/Spark task; for writes, the client pipelines bytes through DataNode 1 → 2 → 3, with replication happening inline. 3. When a DataNode fails (missed heartbeat for 10 seconds), the NameNode marks its chunks under-replicated and instructs surviving replicas to copy themselves to other DataNodes until the replication factor of three is restored — the cluster self-heals without operator intervention.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Mini distributed filesystem mock: a NameNode (metadata) + several DataNodes (chunk storage) with 3x replication, rack-aware placement, and…
- Stores chunk bytes.
- Tracks the namespace tree and chunk -> DataNode mapping.
- Rack-aware placement: 1st on rack A, 2nd on rack B, 3rd on rack A.
- First replica: rack 0. Second: rack 1. Third: rack 0 (different node).
- Pipeline replicate: DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3
- Client prefers the closest (here: first alive) replica
- 5 datanodes across 2 racks

**Defines:** `ChunkInfo`, `FileMeta`, `DataNode`, `NameNode`

```python
"""
Mini distributed filesystem mock: a NameNode (metadata) + several DataNodes
(chunk storage) with 3x replication, rack-aware placement, and self-healing
when a DataNode fails. Demonstrates the GFS/HDFS architecture.
"""
import hashlib, random, time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

CHUNK_SIZE = 128 * 1024 * 1024   # 128 MB, like HDFS default
REPLICATION = 3

@dataclass
class ChunkInfo:
    chunk_id: str
    size: int
    replicas: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # DataNode ids

@dataclass
class FileMeta:
    path: str
    chunks: list[ChunkInfo] = field(default_factory=list)

class DataNode:
    """Stores chunk bytes. Reports heartbeats to the NameNode."""
    def __init__(self, node_id: str, rack: str):
        self.node_id = node_id
        self.rack = rack
        self.chunks: dict[str, bytes] = {}
        self.alive = True
        self.last_heartbeat = time.time()

    def store(self, chunk_id: str, data: bytes):
        self.chunks[chunk_id] = data

    def fetch(self, chunk_id: str) -> bytes:
        return self.chunks[chunk_id]

    def heartbeat(self):
        self.last_heartbeat = time.time()

class NameNode:
    """Tracks the namespace tree and chunk -> DataNode mapping."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.files: dict[str, FileMeta] = {}
        self.datanodes: dict[str, DataNode] = {}
        self._chunk_counter = 0

    def register_datanode(self, dn: DataNode):
        self.datanodes[dn.node_id] = dn

    def _pick_replica_nodes(self, exclude: set[str] = set()) -> list[str]:
        """Rack-aware placement: 1st on rack A, 2nd on rack B, 3rd on rack A."""
        alive = [d for d in self.datanodes.values()
                 if d.alive and d.node_id not in exclude]
        if len(alive) < REPLICATION:
            raise RuntimeError(f"only {len(alive)} datanodes alive, need {REPLICATION}")
        racks = {}
        for d in alive:
            racks.setdefault(d.rack, []).append(d)
        rack_list = list(racks.values())
        random.shuffle(rack_list)
        chosen = []
        # First replica: rack 0. Second: rack 1. Third: rack 0 (different node).
        chosen.append(rack_list[0].pop(0))
        if len(rack_list) > 1:
            chosen.append(rack_list[1].pop(0))
        else:
            chosen.append(rack_list[0].pop(0))
        chosen.append(rack_list[0].pop(0))
        return [c.node_id for c in chosen]

    def write_file(self, path: str, data: bytes):
        """Split into chunks, pick replica nodes, pipeline-replicate each."""
        chunks = [data[i:i + CHUNK_SIZE] for i in range(0, len(data), CHUNK_SIZE)] or [b""]
        self.files[path] = FileMeta(path=path)
        for chunk_bytes in chunks:
            self._chunk_counter += 1
            cid = f"chunk-{self._chunk_counter:04d}"
            replica_ids = self._pick_replica_nodes()
            # Pipeline replicate: DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3
            primary, *secondaries = replica_ids
            self.datanodes[primary].store(cid, chunk_bytes)
            for sid in secondaries:
                self.datanodes[sid].store(cid, chunk_bytes)   # simplified
            self.files[path].chunks.append(
                ChunkInfo(chunk_id=cid, size=len(chunk_bytes), replicas=replica_ids))

    def read_file(self, path: str) -> bytes:
        if path not in self.files:
            raise FileNotFoundError(path)
        out = bytearray()
        for c in self.files[path].chunks:
            # Client prefers the closest (here: first alive) replica
            for dn_id in c.replicas:
                dn = self.datanodes[dn_id]
                if dn.alive:
                    out.extend(dn.fetch(c.chunk_id))
                    break
            else:
                raise RuntimeError(f"chunk {c.chunk_id} has no alive replica!")
        return bytes(out)

    def check_heartbeats(self, timeout: float = 10.0):
        """Mark datanodes dead if they missed heartbeat; re-replicate."""
        now = time.time()
        for dn in self.datanodes.values():
            if dn.alive and (now - dn.last_heartbeat) > timeout:
                print(f"  NameNode: DataNode {dn.node_id} missed heartbeat -> DEAD")
                dn.alive = False
        self._re_replicate()

    def _re_replicate(self):
        """For each under-replicated chunk, copy from a surviving replica."""
        for f in self.files.values():
            for c in f.chunks:
                alive = [r for r in c.replicas if self.datanodes[r].alive]
                if len(alive) < REPLICATION:
                    if not alive:
                        print(f"  NameNode: chunk {c.chunk_id} LOST (no replicas)")
                        continue
                    src = self.datanodes[alive[0]]
                    needed = REPLICATION - len(alive)
                    candidates = [d for d in self.datanodes.values()
                                  if d.alive and d.node_id not in c.replicas]
                    for new_dn in candidates[:needed]:
                        new_dn.store(c.chunk_id, src.fetch(c.chunk_id))
                        c.replicas.append(new_dn.node_id)
                        print(f"  NameNode: re-replicated {c.chunk_id} "
                              f"to {new_dn.node_id} (rf={len(c.replicas)})")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    nn = NameNode()
    # 5 datanodes across 2 racks
    for i, rack in enumerate(["rack-A","rack-B","rack-A","rack-B","rack-A"]):
        nn.register_datanode(DataNode(f"dn-{i+1}", rack))
    for d in nn.datanodes.values():
        d.heartbeat()

    nn.write_file("/logs/app.log", b"event=click user=alice\n" * 10_000)
    print("Wrote /logs/app.log; chunks:",
          [c.chunk_id for c in nn.files["/logs/app.log"].chunks])
    print("Replica placement:",
          [(c.chunk_id, c.replicas) for c in nn.files["/logs/app.log"].chunks])

    # Read back
    data = nn.read_file("/logs/app.log")
    print(f"Read back {len(data)} bytes")

    # Simulate DataNode failure
    print("\nKilling dn-1...")
    nn.datanodes["dn-1"].alive = False
    nn.check_heartbeats()
    print("After healing, replica placement:",
          [(c.chunk_id, c.replicas) for c in nn.files["/logs/app.log"].chunks])

    # Reads still succeed
    data2 = nn.read_file("/logs/app.log")
    print(f"Read back {len(data2)} bytes after failure")
    assert data == data2, "data corrupted!"
    print("PASS: data integrity preserved across node failure")
```

quiz.explanation: The 128MB chunk size is an optimization for the HDFS workload: large sequential reads of big files by MapReduce and Spark. A larger chunk reduces the NameNode's metadata footprint — one chunk ID per 128MB rather than per 4KB means a 1PB cluster has 8M chunks instead of 256B, which fits in NameNode RAM (typically 64–128GB).

A billion 1KB files consumes 150GB of NameNode RAM, far exceeding a typical 64GB heap, while using only 1PB out of a possible 50PB cluster capacity. The cluster becomes unbalanced: NameNode GC pauses, slow namespace operations, RPC congestion.

quiz.explanation: HDFS and CephFS are both distributed filesystems, but they target different workloads. HDFS is purpose-built for Hadoop/Spark batch analytics: 128MB chunks, write-once-read-many, append-only writes (no random write), no POSIX locking, and a single NameNode (or HA pair) that scales to ~100M files before metadata becomes a bottleneck.
